newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mazda expects real Ford synergy benefit after 2000.
newsitem.headline: Mazda expects real Ford synergy benefit after 2000.

text.p: Mazda Motor Corp President Henry Wallace told Reuters on Thursday that he expects the real benefits from synergies with Ford Motor Co will come beyond the year 2000.
Ford holds a one-third share of the Japanese carmaker.
"Real benefit from synergies with Ford will come beyond 2000," Wallace said in an interview.

He said Mazda will unveil the general outline for sharing an automobile platform with Ford in the next week to 10 days, although he gave no details about which models may use the common platform or when platform sharing would be implemented.
He said platform sharing usually includes engines and transmissions, which are critical parts of the vehicle.

Asked what Mazda's earnings results would be for the fiscal year ended on March 31, Wallace said the final results will be published in May, but he expected that Mazda would be pretty close to what it forecast when it announced its interim results in November.
Mazda at that time said it expected to post a net parent profit of six billion yen in 1996/97.
"I expect we're still on track (on the 1996/97 net profit forecast)," he said.
He said although Mazda's sales from October to December were weaker than expected, he was waiting to see the extent to which the stronger dollar may have improved the company's performance.
He said he was pleased with the recent dollar rally, which had helped boost exports and profits at Japan's carmakers.
"I'm not disappointed to see where it (the dollar) is in the marketplace," he said.
He expected the dollar would test the 130 yen level in the short term, but then fall back below 120 yen before the end of this year.
Wallace also said he expected Mazda's business would be stronger in 1997/98 than in the previous year.
"Overall, it will be a better year," he said.
"I think the worst is over, although I think we still have a long way to go as a company before I would be comfortable that we are in good shape," he added.

Wallace did not rule out the possibility of job cuts at Mazda's loss-making North American operations, although he said newspaper reports that Mazda was ready to cut 20 percent of its North American workforce were "pure speculation".
An announcement on consolidation of Mazda's North American units was likely this summer, he said. Turning to Japan-U.S. trade issues, he highlighted the importance of deregulation of Japan's economy.
"Obviously the size of the trade imbalance will continue to be an issue of concern," he said.
"I think debate should be focused more on deregulation within the Japanese economy, which will be a more important issue in the long term," he said.
Asked whether Japan should make greater efforts to open its car market, Wallace said; "It's not just an issue of the car industry. I think it's an issue of industry at large and consumers at large."
